q: The island of Pantelleria dries which grape for its celebrated passito?
exp: Zibibbo is the local name for Muscat of Alexandria. The wine is all dried apricot, fig and orange peel, and the vines are trained low in hollows scooped out of the ground to shelter them from the wind.

q: A Veneto grower copies the Mediterranean islands, spreads his sweet-wine crop on mats in an open yard, and loses the lot to grey mould inside a fortnight. What does drying fruit in the open actually depend on?
opts: Salt blowing in off the sea, which pulls water out through the skins
Hot, dry air and weeks with almost no rain while the berries raisin outdoors
Volcanic ground under the mats, which reflects heat up into the bunches
Fruit picked weeks later than usual, so it reaches the mats half shrivelled already
exp: Sun drying belongs to places where the weeks after picking are hot and reliably rainless, which is why Pantelleria, Andalusia and Cyprus all work that way. A cool damp autumn forces the same job indoors onto racks, where fans and open windows take three or four months to do what island sun does in two weeks, and where any bunch showing mould is pulled off the tray before it reaches its neighbours.

q: A systematic tasting method proceeds in which order?
exp: The order matters because each stage constrains the next. Reaching a conclusion first and then hunting for evidence is the commonest way to taste badly.

q: What is the purpose of tasting to a fixed grid rather than freely?
opts: It shortens the tasting by letting you skip components you have already placed
It removes the need for experience
It guarantees the correct grape and origin once every box is filled in
It forces every component to be assessed
exp: A grid stops you skipping the inconvenient components that do not fit the theory you have already formed. It is a discipline against your own guessing, and it settles nothing by itself.

q: In a blind tasting conclusion, which elements are typically called?
opts: The name of the winemaker and their training
The retail price and the importer on the back label
The producer and the single vineyard the wine came from
exp: Grape, place and approximate age, argued from the evidence gathered. Naming the producer is a party trick rather than the exercise.

q: Why should a taster describe rather than judge in the early stages?
opts: Description gathers evidence; judgement ends the enquiry
Only a certified palate is qualified to judge a wine's quality
exp: Saying good or bad closes the question prematurely. Saying pale ruby with a garnet rim leaves you somewhere to go, and no certificate is required to do it.

q: Palate fatigue during a long tasting is best managed how?
opts: Eating strongly flavoured food to reset the palate between flights
Swallowing more slowly so less alcohol reaches the palate
Spitting, water and breaks between flights
exp: Alcohol accumulates and the palate dulls, so swallowing slowly changes nothing. Spitting is professional practice rather than modesty, and plain water between flights resets more than bread does.

q: Ambient conditions can distort a tasting. Which is most disruptive?
exp: The nose does most of the work, so competing aromas from perfume or cooking ruin an assessment. Daylight and a white surface are aids rather than distractions.

q: Why is a white background used when assessing a wine's appearance?
opts: It is required by the wine laws of most producing countries
A pale surface keeps the glass from warming under the lights
It reduces glare on the glass
It shows the wine's true colour and clarity
exp: Colour read against a patterned or coloured surface is unreliable and comes back distorted. A tilted glass over white paper is the standard arrangement, adopted because it works rather than because anything obliges it.

q: The edge of a red has paled and browned while the core stays deep. What does that suggest?
exp: A young red runs to the edge with its core colour; an older one pales and browns at the rim. It is one of the more reliable visual clues.

q: As a red wine ages, its colour generally moves in which direction?
opts: From tawny toward purple as pigment leaves the skins
It stays where it started once the wine is in bottle
From purple through ruby and garnet toward tawny
exp: Anthocyanins polymerise and drop out over time, and nothing in a sealed bottle adds pigment back. Whites move the opposite way, deepening from pale straw toward gold and amber.

q: The tears or legs running down a glass indicate what?
opts: The overall quality of the wine
exp: They are a surface-tension effect, useful as a rough alcohol signal and worthless as a quality one, despite the folklore that better wines run more slowly.

q: You pour a wine that is visibly cloudy in the glass. What should that prompt?
opts: An unfiltered wine, or microbial spoilage
Extended oak ageing, which leaves fine lees suspended in the wine
A wine fined and filtered bright before it was bottled
exp: Deliberately unfiltered wines can be cloudy by intent, so haze prompts a question rather than a verdict. Confirm on the nose and palate. A wine polished bright on the bottling line is the case a hazy glass argues against, and a wine is racked clear off its barrel lees before bottling, so time in barrel is not the source of the haze.

q: Small crystals in the bottom of a bottle or on the cork are usually what?
opts: Fragments of glass from the bottling line
exp: Tartrates precipitate when a wine is chilled and are tasteless. They alarm guests, so a quiet explanation is part of the job.

q: A deep, opaque colour in a young red most reliably suggests what?
opts: Low alcohol, since a lighter wine cannot carry a deep colour
Thick-skinned grapes, a warm climate or a long maceration
Great age, since red wine darkens steadily in bottle
exp: Colour reflects extraction, grape variety and a warm climate more than it reflects quality, and reds lose depth with age rather than gaining it. A pale wine may be a great Pinot Noir and a black one an ordinary Syrah.

q: A young unoaked white smells of lemon, green apple and elderflower. Those aromas are classed as what?
exp: Primary from the fruit, secondary from winemaking including fermentation and oak, tertiary from age. Sorting them is most of the deductive work.
